root_cause: This is the recurring Windows CC (conditional compilation) build out-of-memory failure (8 prior occurrences in the pattern database since 2026-11-03). The ninja build runs many parallel MSVC link.exe processes on a shared Windows runner with limited physical/virtual memory. When several large link steps (pybind_mock_frontend, _pyopenvino, ov_gpu_unit_tests) are scheduled concurrently, link.exe exhausts available memory and fails with LNK1102. The failure is not caused by the triggering PR's content (a GPU kernel rewrite in group_normalization_ref.cl/.cpp, unrelated to the Windows CC build/link configuration) but by runner resource contention combined with high ninja link parallelism on this job.
recommended_actions: Reduce ninja/link parallelism for the Windows CC job (e.g. set CMAKE_JOB_POOLS or ninja -j with a lower link pool size) specifically for large targets like _pyopenvino and ov_gpu_unit_tests
Move to larger-memory Windows runners for the Windows Conditional Compilation workflow, or split heavy link targets into separate jobs
Enable /DEBUG:FASTLINK or reduce PDB/debug info generation for Release CC builds to lower linker memory footprint
Re-run the failed job (handled externally; this doctor only reports) since this is a known infrastructure-related flake
prevention_strategies: Introduce a dedicated link job pool (CMake JOB_POOLS / Ninja pool) capping concurrent link.exe invocations to 1-2 for large python-binding and unit-test targets on Windows runners. Track Windows runner memory headroom in CI metrics and alert when usage trends high. Consider CCache + separate build/link machine sizing for python bindings vs the rest of the build.
reproduction_steps: N/A - requires a memory-constrained Windows build environment with high ninja parallelism; not reliably reproducible outside the shared CI runner pool.
historical_context: This exact signature (LNK1102 out-of-memory on Windows CC build) has recurred 8 times since 2026-11-03 across different commits/PRs, all tracked under pattern 80cfa127185fbf3e, confirming this is a persistent CI infrastructure capacity issue rather than a code regression introduced by any specific PR.
